newsitem.title: USA: Japanese post strong U.S. vehicle sales gains.
newsitem.headline: Japanese post strong U.S. vehicle sales gains.

text.p: U.S. vehicle sales rose modestly in January over a weak month last year, automakers said Monday, but Japanese firms, aided by a weaker yen, scored bigger gains than General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp.

GM reported a 0.9 percent decline in overall vehicle sales for the month, while Chrysler's total sales rose 1.5 percent. Ford was expected to post a gain of about 2 percent for the month, with higher truck sales offsetting lower car sales, analysts said.

But Honda Motor Co. Ltd. scored a 21.1 percent sales increase, fuelled largely by attractive lease deals on passenger cars. Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. said sales jumped 10.7 percent, with healthy gains in domestic and imported cars.

Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. analyst Ronald Glantz said he expected Japanese automakers to show market share gains of nearly a full point once reports from Ford Motor Co. Toyota Motor Corp. and others come in on Tuesday.

Industry executives say the weakness of the yen against the dollar has allowed Japanese automakers to price vehicles more aggressively than they have in years, putting new pressure on Detroit's Big Three.
"I think it's going to be a good year," said Walter Boomershine, who owns a Honda dealership in Smyrna, Ga.
Honda's January U.S. sales rose to 59,306 cars and trucks from 48,967 a year ago. Honda's domestic car sales increased 19.2 percent while imports rose 47.5 percent.

Chrysler's domestic car sales, helped by higher sales to large customers such as car-rental companies, rose 7.7 percent in January, pushing overall sales to 168,157 vehicles from 165,594 a year ago. Chrysler truck sales fell 0.7 percent.

Steve Torok, Chrysler's executive director of sales and marketing, said he believed the nation's No. 3 automaker can maintain its recent market share gains in the face of the Japanese onslaught but added, "it's getting tougher."
"The currency fluctuation has created a real opportunity for them and they're exploiting it," Torok said. "They're going to be taking business from somebody."

GM said total U.S. vehicle sales in January, including results from Saab Automobile AB, fell to 332,000 cars and trucks from 334,958 a year ago. GM's domestic car sales rose 4 percent while domestic truck sales fell 6.7 percent, a drop the automaker blamed partly on model changeovers.

GM marketing chief Ronald Zarrella said sales results for newly introduced GM models "is a clear indication that we're on the right track and that we can expect to see market share improvements during the second half of the year."

The analysts forecast sales for the month at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 14.2 million units, up from about 14 million a year ago, when blizzards ravaged the East Coast and kept buyers from showrooms.
But it would mark the fourth consecutive month in which the sales rate declined, Glantz said.
"January was discouraging, but I'd want to see a few more months before I make a judgment about the rest of the year," he said.
